paper_title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.

These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. Four-choice tasks assess agents ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits. 1. Introduction Long-term interaction requires large language model (LLM) agents to learn from experience, not merely retain explicit facts and preferences [Shinn et al., 2023, Xu et al., 2026]. Associative and latent memories offer complementary mechanisms for organizing and retaining experience [Gutiérrez et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024, 2025]. Useful personalization depends on inferring user characteristics and preferences from interaction history [Nam et al., 2026, Zhong et al., 2024, Zollo et al., 2025] and deciding when these regularities should guide response. Context and subsequent changes can alter whether an otherwise useful default applies [Jiang et al., 2025, Wood and Rünger, 2016]. Existing benchmarks address complementary parts of this problem. LoCoMo and LongMemEval assess recall and reasoning over extended histories [Maharana et al., 2024, Wu et al., 2024], while MemoryAgentBench adds incremental learning and selective forgetting [Hu et al., 2026a]. Pref Eval examines implicit preference inference and following, while PersonaMem tracks evolving user profiles [Jiang et al., 2025, Zhao et al., 2025]. PERMA and DynamicMem study evolving preferences and habits [Liu et al., 2026, Xie et al., 2026]. BenchPreS and OP-Bench examine when personalization should be withheld [Hu et al., 2026b, Yoon et al., 2026], while MemoryArena and Mem2ActBench connect memory to subsequent action [He et al., 2026, Shen et al., 2026]. These developments make precise evaluation question important: when does the available history justify applying HABIT-Bench Table 1 Capability coverage across representative long-term-memory and personalization benchmarks. , , and denote dedicated, partial, and absent benchmark-level coverage, respectively. Columns cover longitudinal history, weak-evidence induction, memory-guided action, contextual gating, exceptions, temporal drift, and withholding unsupported personalization. Benchmark Long Hist. We introduce HABIT-Bench to study this question. We define habit memory as the ability to infer behavioral defaults from incomplete evidence across sessions and apply them according to their scope, exceptions, temporal validity, and user endorsement. relevant past interaction need not establish valid default. repeated choice may apply only in one context, and an assistants suggestion does not become user preference merely because it appears in the history. The target is the support that memory provides for justified decision, rather than particular memory representation [Rabinowitz et al., 2018, Siththaranjan et al., 2024]. HABIT-Bench constructs synthetic histories using task-oriented dialogue seeds and controlled habit graphs. It contains 114 users, 37,152 sessions, and 3,328 probes across food, finance, software, and travel. The domains cover complementary evidence structures. Food combines repeated choices with contextual contrasts, and Travel tests behavioral-rule recovery and its application to new requests. Finance and Software emphasize reconstructing user-confirmed workflows and tracking their changes across sessions. Candidate actions differ in their use of habits, including applying an outdated choice, extending default beyond its scope, or treating an unaccepted suggestion as an established decision. Memory methods process each users history chronologically and supply context to shared base model. We evaluate eight memory methods alongside retrieval baselines and compressed-history control. The best memory-method macro accuracy is 33.06% with Qwen3-235B-A22B [Yang et al., 2025] and 33.61% with GLM-5.3-Flash [Zeng et al., 2026]. These results are close to the best retrieval baselines, while GLMs compressed-history control reaches 41.98%. Oracle Evidence improves access to relevant observations but still leaves substantial decision errors. The results identify both the reconstruction of habits and their appropriate use as important targets for memory system evaluation. Our contributions are as follows. Capability definition. We formulate habit memory as the joint problem of inferring behavioral defaults and determining when the evidence supports their use. Benchmark construction. We introduce four-domain benchmark with chronological histories, 2 HABIT-Bench annotated habit states and supporting sessions, and human validation of decision recoverability. Evaluation and diagnostics. We compare memory systems under shared answer protocol and provide diagnostic controls for evidence access and downstream decision making. The experiments show that elaborate memory pipelines do not consistently outperform simple retrieval on these tasks. 2. Related Work Long-term memory evaluation. LoCoMo evaluates long-conversation question answering, summarization, and multimodal generation [Maharana et al., 2024], while LongMemEval tests extraction, multi-session and temporal reasoning, updates, and abstention [Wu et al., 2024]. MemoryAgentBench examines retrieval, learning, long-range understanding, and selective forgetting under incremental input [Hu et al., 2026a], and MemOps diagnoses memory operations and their composition [Hao et al., 2026]. Implicit and evolving user modeling. PERMA studies preference formation and refinement [Liu et al., 2026], while DynamicMem evaluates evolving attributes, habits, and preferences across applications [Xie et al., 2026]. HorizonBench constructs graph-controlled preference trajectories with traceable provenance [Li et al., 2026]. RefMem-Bench tests behavioral pattern induction, temporal dynamics, and implicit boundaries from fragmented multimodal evidence [Lin et al., 2026]. HABIT-Bench focuses on whether longitudinal evidence supports behavioral default and its subsequent application. Selective personalization. BenchPreS tests preference application under social and institutional constraints in third-party communication [Yoon et al., 2026]. OP-Bench examines irrelevant memory use, repetition, and sycophancy [Hu et al., 2026b]. HABIT-Bench couples selectivity with weakevidence induction, testing scope, exceptions, temporal validity, and user endorsement. Memory-grounded agent behavior. MemoryArena evaluates experience reuse across interdependent sessions [He et al., 2026], and Mem2ActBench tests memory-dependent tool selection and parameter grounding [Shen et al., 2026]. PersonaTrail studies personalized web navigation [Yang et al., 2026], while PersonalAligns AndroidIntent evaluates intent resolution and proactive GUI assistance [Lyu et al., 2026]. IBA-Bench connects implicit user modeling to task execution under enduring traits and transient states [Song et al., 2026]. HABIT-Bench uses non-interactive action selection with shared answer LLM to compare the context produced by different memory systems. Table 1 compares these evaluation targets. 3. We use cooking dialogues and recipes from CookDial [Jiang et al., 2023] to create conversational evidence of preparation and serving habits. Earlier alternatives, later user selections, and repeated use establish behavioral defaults. Contrasting contexts and local exceptions determine their scope. Finance. We use banking dialogues from MultiDoGO [Peskov et al., 2019] to construct histories of financial tasks. Ordered shortlists and later user confirmations establish or replace standing choices. Twoand three-habit probes combine workflows at current or historical times, with local exceptions, unresolved cases, and unaccepted suggestions providing competing evidence. Software. The Software histories use technical-support dialogues from MultiDoGO [Peskov et al., 2019]. Each user has consistent software environment. We use the same selection process as Finance, with more frequent changes to the chosen procedures. The histories also include similar errors in different environments and unfinished support cases. Questions combine two or three habits and may require continuing an earlier case. Travel. Taskmaster-2 [Byrne et al., 2019] flight and hotel dialogues supply behavioral candidates for synthetic user profiles. Alternatives are designed to meet the requests hard constraints while differing in habit use and validity. We check that the choices cover the request, the evidence supports the intended decision, and the context is consistent. Domain-specific structural checks, model-based checks, and human review also assess whether choice can be identified without using the history. Human Validation Human validation tests whether the intended decision is recoverable from the annotated evidence, independently of memory systems ability to find that evidence in long history. Two human reviewers, and B, independently inspect the request, four alternatives, and chronological evidence packet without seeing the gold answer or system predictions. They select the uniquely supported action and assess eight criteria covering answerability, evidence sufficiency, scope, boundaries and exceptions, choice balance, naturalness, source grounding, and privacy. An item without uniquely defensible answer receives no choice rather than forced guess. third human reviewer, C, adjudicates disagreements in either the answer or quality judgments before the merged record is frozen and compared with the gold labels. Appendix details the protocol, sampling, and domain-specific results. Independent review covers 200 Food, 340 Finance, 311 Software, and 618 Travel probes. A/B answer agreement over jointly valid choices is 99.50%, 100.00%, 99.68%, and 92.84%, respectively, with domain-specific denominators and Cohens 𝜅 reported in Appendix Table 6. The quality rubric is stricter than agreement with gold: four Finance items initially receive Modify because their alternatives omit an additional output-placement requirement, although the evidence supports the intended habit. These local issues were corrected before final evaluation, while the audit retains the original modification flags. The remaining 336 Finance items and all 311 Software items pass adjudication. All 79 content-revised Travel items pass targeted gold-blind validation, and all 200 reviewed Food items pass naturalness checks after naturalization. High independent agreement and the rubrics ability to detect narrow construction defects support the quality of the reviewed evidence and decision labels. These checks assess decision recoverability given the evidence, not human retrieval from full histories. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Systems and models. We organize the comparison by the role of memory in each system: controls, retrieval baselines, memory methods, and multi-store memory methods. The No Memory and Full Memory controls omit the interaction history or provide compressed history, respectively. The retrieval baselines select sessions directly from the history and comprise Recency-5, Recency-10, BM25 RAG, Dense RAG, and Temporal Hybrid RAG. The memory methods construct and maintain their own 6 HABIT-Bench memory representations: A-MEM [Xu et al., 2026], Mem0 [Chhikara et al., 2025], MemOS [Li et al., 2025], MemRL [Zhang et al., 2026], LightMem [Fang et al., 2026], and SeCom [Pan et al., 2025]. Letta [Packer et al., 2023] and MIRIX [Wang and Chen, 2025] are shown separately as multi-store memory methods, reflecting their coordination of distinct memory stores. The other six are grouped for presentation rather than treated as single architecture. References to the eight memory methods include both groups. Qwen3-235B-A22B [Yang et al., 2025] and GLM-5.3-Flash [Zeng et al., 2026] are the two primary language models. Within each setting, all methods use the same model to select an answer and to perform memory operations that require an LLM. Dense retrieval components use fixed BGE-M3 encoder [Chen et al., 2025]. Together with additional controls, oracle diagnostics, and experiments with smaller Qwen3 models, the evaluation covers 308 configurations across methods, models, and domains. Inference protocol. Methods maintain separate memory for each user and process sessions in chronological order, using only the history available at each probes visibility cutoff. We set the decoding temperature to zero. The two primary model settings use the same prompt for selecting an action and require outputs to follow fixed JSON schema. In the GLM experiments, the Qwen3-8B tokenizer is used only to measure token budgets, not to generate memories or answers. Context construction and token budgets vary by method. We report accuracy over all probes within each domain and macro accuracy as the unweighted mean of the four domain accuracies. Appendix reports supplementary accuracy averaged across users and, where available, bootstrap confidence intervals obtained by resampling users. It also provides the model configurations, decision prompts, token budgets, and rules for truncation, retries, and answer parsing. Baselines and oracle controls. Retrieval baselines use the request alone, without the answer alternatives, to select complete sessions from the visible history. No Memory omits the interaction history, while Full Memory supplies compacted history that fits within its context budget. Oracle Evidence supplies the private annotated evidence, whereas Oracle Habit State supplies the private habit state and required action. Both oracle conditions use information unavailable to the evaluated methods and serve only as diagnostic controls. 4.2. Main Results Table 3 evaluates whether current memory systems can infer habits from longitudinal weak evidence and apply them to subsequent decisions. Three findings emerge across the two primary model settings. Habit induction and action selection remain challenging. Across the eight memory methods, four-domain macro accuracy ranges from 27.01% to 33.06% with Qwen3-235B-A22B and from 30.42% to 33.61% with GLM-5.3-Flash. Even the best configurations achieve only approximately one-third accuracy, despite using the primary model for both memory operations and action selection. The task requires selecting one of four actions and is scored by exact match, without an LLM judge. The model need not formulate free-form response, but must still distinguish actions supported by the users history from plausible yet unsupported alternatives. Habit-conditioned decision making remains demanding evaluation target across the tested memory designs and model settings. The benefit of memory depends on the domain. Under Qwen3-235B-A22B, the best memorymethod results improve over No Memory by 20.32 percentage points on Food and 13.07 points on Travel. In Finance, all eight methods fall below the 23.54% No Memory point estimate. In Software, the largest gain is 1.03 percentage points. The domain contrast also appears with GLM: the best memory-method accuracies are 28.29% on Finance and 25.44% on Software, compared with 54.62% on Travel. Travel 28.31 55.54 99.23 4.3. Diagnostic Controls and Evidence Analysis Annotated evidence leaves substantial decision difficulty. Under Qwen3-235B-A22B, Oracle Evidence achieves 39.2658.25% accuracy across domains, while Oracle Habit State achieves 98.4199.26%  (Table 4)  . The same qualitative separation appears with Qwen3-8B. Supplying the annotated evidence therefore does not by itself resolve the task. Oracle Habit State additionally exposes the private active state and required action, demonstrating that the answerer can map this privileged information to the correct alternative. The comparison diagnoses remaining difficulty after evidence selection, while combining differences in reconstruction requirements and supplied information. Evidence access and decision correctness remain distinct. For the six source-attributed Qwen3-32B methods, Hit@5 ranges from 37.77% to 41.44%, and annotated-evidence recall from 11.17% to 13.89% (Appendix E.5 Table 13). Hit@5 indicates whether any of the first five attributed sessions is annotated as positive evidence. Evidence recall measures the fraction of the annotated set covered by these sessions. The joint accuracy of the answer and the evidence (Joint A+E) is 12.92-16.20%, requiring correct answer and at least one evidence hit. Clean Grounded@5 is 5.49-8.20% on its eligible subset and additionally requires that none of the attributed sessions be labeled nonbinding. This stricter condition describes the composition of the attributed context. It does not directly measure whether the answerer improperly follows retrieved suggestion. These diagnostics distinguish evidence access, answer correctness, and the exclusion of nonbinding observations, without interpreting an evidence hit as complete reasoning support or differences between eligible subsets as an error decomposition. This distinction matters when the decisive information is distributed across sessions. Retrieving users later selection may be insufficient if an earlier session defines the alternatives, just as retrieving an established default may be insufficient without subsequent exception or replacement. An evidence hit can therefore identify relevant observation without establishing which action is justified at the probes target time. The diagnostic goal is to assess whether the retrieved context supports the complete decision, including the conditions under which the remembered behavior applies. The capability slices in Appendix provide complementary analysis. Method rankings vary across temporal resolution, provenance, reference reconstruction, induction, and exception handling. Strong relative performance on one requirement does not imply the same ordering on another. Overall accuracy should thus be read alongside these diagnostics, which identify distinct demands on memory without attributing every error to retrieval or to habit induction alone. 4.4. Retrieval quantity and ingestion granularity. We conduct separate Qwen3-8B sensitivity study on eight fixed users per domain, covering 32 users and 954 probes, with adapted A-MEM, Mem0, Letta, and MemRL configurations. We vary retrieval top-𝑘 over 2, 5, 10, and 20 at 4096-token ingestion target, and vary the ingestion target over 128, 512, 2048, and 4096 tokens at 𝑘 = 5, using each methods native tokenizer. Figure 3(a) reports the equal-domain mean of probe-level accuracies from the recorded run aggregates. Accuracy ranges from 24.83% to 31.71% across the tested settings. Increasing 𝑘 from 2 to 20 raises A-MEM from 29.23% to 31.21% and Letta from 28.53% to 31.71%, while larger ingestion chunks do not consistently improve accuracy. Thus, varying retrieval quantity or ingestion granularity alone does not remove the observed limitations on this cohort. Memory construction and query costs. Figure 3(b) separates memory construction from subsequent retrieval and answering across ten methods on the same cohort. The recorded per-user measurements sum to 54.59 hours and 107.80 million LLM tokens for A-MEM construction, compared with 13.24 minutes and 3.39 million tokens for its queries. This illustrates the substantial upfront cost that 10 HABIT-Bench memory construction can incur even when subsequent queries are relatively inexpensive. Time is accumulated per-user latency, not parallel job wall time, and tokens include LLM prompts and completions but exclude embeddings. Initialization and discarded failed or interrupted runs are excluded. These measurements characterize the recorded implementations rather than matched accuracycost ranking or an extrapolation to the full dataset. Separating construction from querying is important because memory is reused across subsequent requests. low query cost can conceal substantial processing of the preceding history, while the value of that investment depends on how often the resulting memory is consulted and updated. The sensitivity and cost analyses therefore address complementary questions: how retrieval and ingestion choices affect decisions, and where computation is spent over the memory lifecycle. 5. Conclusion HABIT-Bench evaluates whether agents can infer behavioral defaults from longitudinal weak evidence and use them to make context-appropriate decisions. Its four domains require agents to integrate distributed observations while tracking applicability, exceptions, temporal validity, and user endorsement. Across the evaluated configurations, memory benefits vary substantially by domain, and richer memory pipelines do not consistently outperform retrieval or budget-feasible history compression. Oracle controls show that supplying annotated evidence still leaves substantial decision difficulty, while evidence-attribution diagnostics distinguish partial retrieval from grounded action selection. These findings motivate memory representations that preserve the relationships between default, its supporting observations, and its conditions of validity. HABIT-Bench provides controlled setting for studying how such representations support context-appropriate decisions.

sections.content: A. Domain-specific Construction and Validation The four domains share chronological user histories and deterministic four-choice interface, while differing in their source tasks, evidence structures, and habit composition. The following sections describe the construction and validation of the evaluated datasets. A.1. Food Templates and source compatibility. The Food pipeline starts with 20 habit templates for private preparation, finishing, and serving choices. Each template specifies its applicability condition, default action, competing action, boundary condition/action, and exception condition/action. Illustrative axes include the placement of herbs, chili, and briny accents, as well as recipe finishing styles. Templates that are effectively generic safety rules are filtered out. Trigger patterns constrain assignment to compatible recipe seeds, so that an oven-related habit is not inserted into an unrelated cooking task. The dialogue and recipe seeds come from CookDial [Jiang et al., 2023]. User continuity, habit assignments, and probe labels are constructed within HABIT-Bench rather than inherited from CookDial. Evidence scheduling. Each user receives seven habits. stable habit has ten signal sessions: one candidate shortlist, one distant ordinal resolution, three ratified reuses, two boundary observations, one one-case exception, one nonresolving rehearsal, and one rejected assistant suggestion. Key signals are distributed across early, middle, and late history. The boundary observations deliberately include weak positive and an adjacent near-boundary negative: the contrast is locally available even though the overall habit evidence is longitudinal. This is not claim that every supporting observation is far from every other observation. Sixty ordinary sessions are added to the 70 signal sessions, giving 130 sessions per user and 3,900 sessions in total. Naturalization and probes. Naturalization rewrites planned sessions into cooking conversations while preserving recipe facts and habit evidence. Validation checks turn limits, protected recipe numbers, evidence-index alignment, preference leakage in ordinary sessions, mechanical phrasing, and benchmark-related terms. Each of the 210 user-level habits yields direct-use, boundary, and exception probes. Query surfaces reduce direct overlap with reuse evidence, and all four alternatives are adapted to the current scenario so that the gold action is not the only physically applicable option. The final dataset contains 630 probes. Exception scope and validation. Exceptions authorize local departure from the default rather than durable replacement. The decision target distinguishes applying the default, respecting its boundary, and following the exception in its applicable context. Naturalization and human validation are part of the construction pipeline, with review criteria and results reported in Appendix B. A.2. Finance Source transformation and persona consistency. The Finance source from MultiDoGO [Peskov et al., 2019] contains 8,832 conversations and 157,229 utterances. Conversations are reconstructed by identifier and turn order, then assigned primary task intent. They supply task types, slot categories, interaction patterns, and style exemplars, while original identities and sensitive financial fields are replaced in the synthetic lifelines. The resulting 17,405 source-linked sessions use 7,049 primary source conversations, with no primary seed used more than three times. Source-linked and evidence-annotated sessions are overlapping categories. 15 HABIT-Bench Each of the 36 users has stable banking persona, including synthetic account identifiers and consistent financial background. The history has 540 sessions per user, spanning January 2021 through June 2025. The final 19,440 sessions include 16,180 without memory annotations and 3,260 with some annotation; annotation is not synonymous with decisive evidence. Habit state and evidence topology. There are eight candidate habits. Each user activates six and leaves two absent; two active habits undergo replacement. Workflow variants cover money movement, card/account changes, minimal secure verification, urgent fraud handling, account-review presentation, dispute preparation, noncommittal credit/loan analysis, and current payment-status checks. The secure-verification habit is active for every Finance user. Variants are designed to distinguish user-specific processes rather than safe versus plainly unsafe alternatives. standing policy is recovered by joining an ordered shortlist with distant user resolution that refers to an ordinal alternative. For drift habits, an additional shortlist/resolution pair establishes replacement. One-off cases, unaccepted assistant proposals, unresolved rehearsals, and tentative signals are not automatically binding. Probe evidence must link each task component to the appropriate workstream, policy pair, user resolution, and target time. The private chains distinguish decisive, temporal-context, and nonbinding evidence. Probe construction and validation. The 1,368 probes comprise 944 two-habit and 424 threehabit decisions. Types include as-of reversals, interleaved temporal composition, surface-decoy pairs, reference-case reconstruction, suggestion rejection, provenance-sensitive composition, and scope/temporal pairs. Validation checks goldgraph consistency, querychoice completeness, evidence topology, and surface quality. In particular, choices must cover every required task component, with no component supplied only by the gold alternative. The dataset also defines 288 decision units for complementary unit-level aggregation. Human review retains 336 of 340 sampled items and identifies four querychoice coverage defects, which are corrected before final evaluation (Appendix B). A.3. Software Source transformation and environments. The Software source from MultiDoGO [Peskov et al., 2019] contains 5,562 conversations and 86,220 utterances. Task intents are inferred from complete conversations. The resulting 8,678 source-linked sessions use 2,828 primary conversations, with at most four realizations per primary seed. They retain support-task structure, slot categories, clarification patterns, and expression styles while replacing original company identities, credentials, contact fields, and repetitive helpdesk language. Each synthetic user has consistent organization, operating system, browser, product suite, support account, and work context. Habit assignment and temporal interference. Eighteen users each have 540 sessions, giving 9,720 sessions: 8,014 without memory annotations and 1,706 with some annotation. Seventeen users have six active habits and one has five. The seven candidate habits concern diagnostics, documentation lookup, escalation thresholds, secure account recovery, platform-specific instructions, backup before risky changes, and receipts after actual ticket submission. Software shares Finances distant shortlist/resolution mechanism and contains 71 replacement chains. Drift frequency varies across users: nine have two replacements each, eight have six, and one has five. Competing evidence includes similar errors in different environments, case-local diagnostic routes, unaccepted proposals, and prior unresolved checkpoints. Ticket receipts are scoped to submitted tickets, not merely drafts or ongoing troubleshooting. Probe construction and validation. The 680 probes comprise 464 two-habit and 216 three-habit decisions. They combine workflow selection with temporal state, provenance, and reference-case 16 HABIT-Bench continuation. Validation checks querychoice coverage, goldgraph consistency, and nonredundant query text. The dataset defines 161 decision units, and human review accepts all 311 sampled items (Appendix B). A.4. Travel Source-derived motifs and history-first realization. Travel begins with independent flight and hotel conversations from Taskmaster-2 [Byrne et al., 2019]. Source conversations provide behavioral motifs rather than cross-conversation user identities. Semantic consolidation yields 47 grounded instances, 18 policy prototypes across 13 habit families, and 194 habits assigned to 30 synthetic users. Each user is specified by dossier and chronological arc. Natural multi-turn sessions are authored before evidence annotation and blind recoverability checks, so the history establishes the habit before the probe tests its application. The histories contain 4,092 sessions, with 124147 per user: 790 evidence-mode and 3,302 ordinary-mode sessions. There are 194 initial habit states and eight revisions within the lifelines. Probe-visible sessions are restricted by their chronological cutoffs. Decision probes. The dataset contains 650 probes: 456 single-habit and 194 two-habit decisions. Probe families include cross-context transfer, conflict resolution, evidence disambiguation, exception/default composition, scope composition, and temporal-state composition. Private annotations specify the relevant habits and evidence for each decision. The query and alternatives provide current candidate facts, while historical sessions establish the user-specific behavioral rule needed to choose among them. Validation and evaluation scope. Validation combines gold-blind, history-informed answerability checks with history-free checks for generic-best shortcuts. and independently assess the sampled items, adjudicates disagreements, and content revisions receive targeted blind review. Appendix reports agreement and review coverage. The experiments evaluate the full probe set with user-isolated memories and chronological cutoffs. Travel is controlled diagnostic set, not an independently sequestered generalization test. A.5. Cross-domain Interpretation The common four-choice interface does not make the evidence mechanisms identical. Food includes both split decisions and repeated reuse, with local contrast for boundaries. Finance and Software predominantly test cross-session decision reconstruction and policy-state maintenance. Travel emphasizes behavioral-rule recovery and compositional application. The benchmark therefore evaluates integration of incomplete longitudinal evidence, not exclusively statistical inference from unratified behavior. Likewise, deterministic action labels do not establish probabilistic habit-calibration task. These distinctions should constrain both the capability claims and the interpretation of domain-averaged accuracy. B. Human Validation Protocol and Results B.1.
